extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of complex analysis (advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and worked examples on residues, contour integration, classification of isolated singularities, meromorphic functions, the argument principle, homotopy/simply-connected domains, and branches of the complex logarithm. Includes theorems, proofs, and contour-choosing guidance for evaluating integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue formula (single pole)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic in an open set containing a circle C and its interior except for a pole at z0 inside C, then ∮_C f(z) dz = 2πi·res_{z0} f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The residue is the coefficient a_{-1} in the Laurent expansion of f about z0. The result follows by integrating the principal part; the holomorphic part integrates to 0 by Cauchy's theorem. This is the basis for computing many improper real integrals via contour integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue formula (multiple poles / toy contours)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic in an open set containing a circle (or toy contour) and its interior except for finitely many poles z1,...,zN inside, then ∮_C f(z) dz = 2πi·∑_{k=1}^N res_{zk} f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses keyhole/multiple-keyhole contours that avoid poles and then shrinks corridors so the large contour integral equals sum of small circle integrals. Orientation of γ is taken positive. Applicable equally to toy contours after choosing an appropriate keyhole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of residues (simple poles)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a simple pole at z0, res_{z0} f = lim_{z→z0} (z−z0)f(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in examples: e.g., f(z)=1/(1+z^2) has simple poles at ±i; residue at i computed as 1/(2i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of residues (higher order poles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Residues at poles of order m can be computed using Cauchy integral formulae for derivatives / derivative formulas from Laurent coefficients (i.e., take appropriate (m−1)th derivative after multiplying by (z−z0)^m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text references using formulas for derivatives (Corollary 4.2, previous chapter). Practically: res = 1/(m−1)! · lim_{z→z0} d^{m−1}/dz^{m−1}[(z−z0)^m f(z)].

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy for evaluating real improper integrals via residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend the integrand f(x) to a meromorphic function f(z) on the complex plane and choose a family of toy contours γ_R so that lim_{R→∞} ∮_{γ_R} f(z) dz equals the real integral ∫_{−∞}^{∞} f(x) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main challenge is choosing γ_R so integrals over auxiliary parts vanish; the choice is motivated by decay behavior of f. Examples: semicircles for rational-decay integrands, rectangles for functions with exponential/periodic structure, or strips when function has periodicity in imaginary direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contour selection and decay estimates (vanishing arc integrals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select contours (large semicircles, vertical sides of rectangles, etc.) so that integrals on those parts tend to zero as R→∞, often by bounding |f(z)| and using decay rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical bounding: if |f(z)| ≤ B/|z|^2 on a large arc C_R^+, then |∮_{C_R^+} f(z) dz| ≤ (πR)(B/R^2)=O(1/R)→0. For vertical sides use estimates like Ce^{(a−1)R} when a<1, etc. Ensure estimates match chosen contour and function growth/decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using periodicity / vertical-rectangle contours for exponential/periodic integrands
rubrics_metrics.description: For integrands involving e^{az} or functions with imaginary-periodicity (e.g., e^{z} periodic in vertical translation), use a rectangular contour whose vertical height matches the period to relate integrals on top and bottom sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: f(z)=e^{az}/(1+e^z) integrated over a rectangle of height 2π yields relation between bottom integral I and top integral −e^{2πia}I; compute residue of pole inside rectangle (e.g., at πi) and let vertical side integrals vanish by growth estimates dependent on a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using fixed-height rectangles for Fourier / transform integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: For Fourier-type integrals with integrands having poles at discrete imaginary shifts, use a rectangle of fixed height (matching period) whose width→∞ so vertical integrals vanish and top side equals factor times bottom integral due to periodicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: f(z)=e^{−2πizξ}/cosh(πz) uses rectangle of height 2 with poles at i/2,3i/2. Compute residues and use cosh periodicity to relate integrals; bound vertical integrals by showing denominator grows like e^{πR}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann's theorem on removable singularities
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic in an open set Ω except possibly at z0 and f is bounded on Ω\\{z0}, then z0 is a removable singularity (f can be redefined so it is holomorphic at z0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct primitive via adapted toy-contour and use integral representation f(z)=1/(2πi)∮_C f(ζ)/(ζ−z) dζ for z in disc to define extension; boundedness ensures vanishing contribution of small-circle integral as radius→0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of poles via blow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: An isolated singularity z0 is a pole iff |f(z)|→∞ as z→z0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via consideration of 1/f: if |f|→∞ then 1/f→0 so 1/f has removable singularity and zeros at z0, hence f has a pole; conversely if pole then 1/f has zero and f blows up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of isolated singularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Every isolated singularity is either removable (f bounded), a pole (|f|→∞), or essential (neither of the previous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential singularities exhibit 'wild' behavior (Casorati-Weierstrass and Picard). Use Laurent expansion to identify type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casorati–Weierstrass theorem (essential singularities)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has an essential singularity at z0 then the image of any punctured neighborhood Dr(z0)\{z0} under f is dense in C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume image misses a disc around w, consider g=1/(f−w) which is bounded, hence removable; derive contradiction by analyzing behavior at z0. Picard's theorem strengthens this further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of meromorphic function (finite isolated poles)
rubrics_metrics.description: f is meromorphic on open set Ω if there is a sequence of points {z_k} with no limit points in Ω such that f is holomorphic on Ω\{z_k} and has poles at the z_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also define meromorphic on the extended plane by examining behavior at infinity via f(1/z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meromorphic on extended plane ⇔ rational functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A function meromorphic on the extended complex plane (i.e., only finitely many poles including possibly at ∞) is a rational function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: subtract principal parts (polynomials in 1/(z−z_k)) at all poles (including ∞); the remainder is entire and bounded hence constant by Liouville; reconstruct f as rational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is meromorphic in an open set containing a circle C and its interior and f has no zeros or poles on C, then (1/2πi)∮_C f'(z)/f(z) dz = (number of zeros of f inside C) − (number of poles of f inside C), counted with multiplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key fact: f'/f has simple poles at zeros and poles of f with residues equal to their orders (zeros give +n, poles give −n). Use residue theorem to obtain the count. Useful for counting zeros and in proofs of Rouché.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue of f'/f equals multiplicity sign
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has a zero of order n at z0, res_{z0} (f'/f) = n; if f has a pole of order n at z0, res_{z0} (f'/f) = −n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write f(z)=(z−z0)^n g(z) with g holomorphic and nonvanishing; compute f'/f = n/(z−z0) + g'/g to read off the residue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rouché's theorem (counting zeros under perturbation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are holomorphic in an open set containing circle C and its interior and |f(z)| > |g(z)| for all z∈C, then f and f+g have the same number of zeros inside C (counted with multiplicity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via continuous family f_t=f+tg and argument principle: number of zeros is integer-valued and continuous in t under the inequality (no zeros on C), so constant. Use this to perturb functions without changing zero counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open mapping theorem for holomorphic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic and non-constant in a region Ω, then f maps open sets to open sets (f is an open map).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: near z0 with w0=f(z0), write g(z)=f(z)−w and apply Rouché on small disc to show nearby values w are in the image. Consequence: holomorphic non-constant maps cannot collapse open sets to lower-dimensional sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum modulus principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is non-constant and holomorphic in a region Ω, then |f| cannot attain a maximum in the interior of Ω.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open mapping: if f attained interior maximum at z0, f would map small neighborhood to a neighborhood of f(z0), contradicting maximality. Corollary: for compact closure, supremum is attained on boundary unless f is constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homotopy invariance of integrals of holomorphic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic in Ω and γ0,γ1 are homotopic curves in Ω with same endpoints, then ∫_{γ0} f(z) dz = ∫_{γ1} f(z) dz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs finite cover of intermediate curves by discs where local primitives exist; uses cancellation of constants of integration on overlaps. This underlies deformation of contours in contour integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simply connected domain ⇔ primitives exist globally
rubrics_metrics.description: A region Ω is simply connected if any two curves with same endpoints are homotopic. If Ω is simply connected and f is holomorphic, then f has a primitive on Ω and hence ∮_γ f = 0 for all closed γ in Ω (Cauchy's theorem in simply connected domains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct primitive F(z)=∫_{γ} f(w) dw from fixed basepoint; independence of path follows from simple connectivity. Use this to define single-valued branches of primitives like the logarithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstruction example: punctured plane not simply connected
rubrics_metrics.description: The punctured plane C\{0} is not simply connected — e.g., ∮_{unit circle} 1/z dz = 2πi ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that 1/z has no single-valued primitive on C\{0}; motivates introducing branches on simply connected subdomains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branch of complex logarithm on simply connected domain
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is simply connected, 1∈Ω and 0∉Ω, then there exists a holomorphic branch log_Ω(z) satisfying (i) log_Ω' = 1/z, (ii) e^{log_Ω z}=z, (iii) log_Ω(r)=log r for real r near 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct log_Ω as primitive of 1/z via path integration from 1 to z; principal branch obtained on slit plane C\(−∞,0] with argument in (−π,π). Note log(z1 z2) may fail globally due to branch choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor expansion for principal log and complex powers
rubrics_metrics.description: On |z|<1, principal log has expansion log(1+z)=∑_{n=1}^∞ (−1)^{n+1} z^n/n. Define z^α = e^{α log z} once a branch of log is chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivative-check argument shows equality of series; when defining powers, choose branch of log on simply connected domain not containing 0 to make z^α single-valued there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of holomorphic logarithm for nowhere-vanishing functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is nowhere vanishing and holomorphic in simply connected Ω, then there exists holomorphic g with f(z)=e^{g(z)} (i.e., a holomorphic log f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct g(z)=∫_{γ} f'(w)/f(w) dw + c0 with ec0=f(z0). Independence of path follows from simple connectivity. This is the generalization of the branch of log to functions.
